1011.quote_or_event: “Make modesty your circumcision, and good conduct your fast. In this way, you shall be a true Muslim.”
1011.explanation: Speaking to Muslims in Majh ki Vaar, Guru Nanak turns outward religious marks into inner virtues, making saram (modesty, recoil from wrong) the real sign of faith.
1011.tie_back: The Kural separates true shame, recoil from a wrong deed, from customary bashfulness; Guru Nanak likewise sets inward modesty above the outward form.
1011.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 140, Raag Majh, Majh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1011._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both value inner modesty over outward form, but Guru Nanak contrasts it with ritual, while the Kural contrasts it with women's customary bashfulness.

1012.quote_or_event: “Make virtue your bread, good conduct the ghee, and modesty the meat to eat.”
1012.explanation: In a salok of Bihaagra ki Vaar headed Mardana 1 (traditionally Guru Nanak addressing his companion Bhai Mardana), the ordinary staples of life are turned into virtues, with modesty as the meat of the meal.
1012.tie_back: The Kural says food and clothing are common to all beings and that shame is what sets good people apart; the salok makes modesty itself the true food of a human life.
1012.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 553, Raag Bihaagra, Bihaagra ki Vaar (salok headed Mardana 1) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1012._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on putting modesty above bodily needs; authorship of this salok is given as Guru Nanak in tradition but BaniDB lists Bhai Mardana, and the verse does not claim that modesty marks off humans from other beings.

1013.quote_or_event: “Modesty and righteousness both, O Nanak, are qualities of those who are blessed with true wealth.”
1013.explanation: Guru Nanak pairs saram (modesty) with dharam (righteousness), as two qualities that dwell together in those who are truly rich.
1013.tie_back: The Kural says noble character dwells in shame as life dwells in the body; Guru Nanak likewise treats modesty as the companion and seat of righteousness.
1013.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1287, Raag Malaar, Malaar ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1013._accuracy_note: Partial: Sant Singh Khalsa's translation supports the pairing of modesty and virtue, but Prof. Sahib Singh reads this line as quoting the worldly view that wealth secures honour, so the parallel depends on the translation.

1014.quote_or_event: “Ego is a chronic disease, but it contains its own cure as well.”
1014.explanation: In a salok of Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad calls haumai (ego), the root problem in Sikh teaching, a long-lasting disease that can still be cured through the Guru's grace.
1014.tie_back: The Kural says that without shame the proud, stately walk of the great is a sickness; Guru Angad names that pride, ego, as the disease itself.
1014.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 466, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1014._accuracy_note: Matches the Kural's second line, pride as disease, but does not mention shame as an ornament, which is the first half of the couplet.

1015.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
1015.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the state reached in the company of the holy, in which no one is felt to be other than oneself.
1015.tie_back: The Kural praises those who feel another's disgrace as keenly as their own; Guru Arjan's refusal to count anyone a stranger is the outlook from which such shared shame grows.
1015.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1015._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it gives the sense of oneness that underlies the Kural's idea, but says nothing about shame or disgrace.

1016.quote_or_event: “If I were to become an emperor and raise a huge army, and sit on a throne, issuing commands and collecting taxes-O Nanak, all of this could pass away like a puff of wind.”
1016.explanation: Guru Nanak imagines himself given an emperor's throne and power, and refuses to value it if it would make him forget the Name.
1016.tie_back: The Kural says the great would not want the whole wide world at the price of their hedge of shame; Guru Nanak would not want a whole empire at the price of forgetting God.
1016.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 14, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1016._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the structure (refusing the world for something higher) is shared, but Guru Nanak's higher good is remembrance of the Name, not shame.

1017.quote_or_event: “those who merely live shall depart in dishonor; everything they eat is impure.”
1017.explanation: In Majh ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says that a life that goes on after its honour (pat) is lost is worthless, and everything it consumes is tainted.
1017.tie_back: The Kural says those who live by shame will give up life rather than shame; Guru Nanak says that life kept at the cost of honour is not worth living.
1017.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Majh, Majh ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1017._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on honour above mere survival; the commentators link the lost honour to living without the Name, so this is about spiritual honour rather than the Kural's sense of shame as such.

1018.quote_or_event: “Modesty and righteousness both have vanished, and falsehood struts around like a leader, O Lalo.”
1018.explanation: Describing the sack of Saidpur in his Babarvani hymns, Guru Nanak tells his disciple Lalo that saram (modesty) and dharam (righteousness) have both gone into hiding.
1018.tie_back: The Kural warns that when a person loses shame, virtue itself is ashamed and leaves; Guru Nanak shows modesty and righteousness leaving together.
1018.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1018._accuracy_note: Strong fit on modesty and virtue departing together; Guru Nanak speaks of a whole society in a time of violence, while the Kural speaks of a single person.

1019.quote_or_event: “Modesty has left her home, and honor has gone away with her.”
1019.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak pictures modesty walking out of the house and honour following her.
1019.tie_back: The Kural says that once shamelessness settles in it burns away every good thing; Guru Nanak shows the same chain, with honour going the moment modesty leaves.
1019.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1243, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1019._accuracy_note: Strong fit on losing shame and then everything else; the Kural's contrast between a lapse that harms the family and shamelessness that harms all is not in the verse.

1020.quote_or_event: “How does the puppet of clay dance?”
1020.explanation: Bhagat Ravidas, whose hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, marvels at the human body, a puppet of clay, dancing about as if under its own power while it is pulled by worldly attachment.
1020.tie_back: The Kural compares the shameless to a wooden puppet on strings that only seems alive; Ravidas uses the same image of a puppet that dances while having no life of its own.
1020.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 487, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Ravidas (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1020._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the puppet image is close, but Ravidas applies it to every mortal caught in Maya, not specifically to people without shame, and the Kural's pun on naan (shame and string) has no parallel.
